Kaposiform Hemangioendothelioma

Neoplastic MONDO:0016236 Pathograph 18 Show in embeddings browser hemangioendothelioma soft tissue neoplasm

Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma (KHE) is a rare vascular tumour of infancy and early childhood, of intermediate type: locally aggressive, it infiltrates skin, fat, muscle and bone, without distant metastasis. Its endothelium carries lymphatic markers. The cause of most tumours is unknown; a somatic activating GNA14 variant has been reported in one KHE in the cited studies, and whether it causes the tumour is not known. Its best-known complication, the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, in which platelets are trapped and consumed inside the tumour, is reported in 42% to 78% of patients across the KHE series cited here (40% where tufted angioma is pooled in) and is curated separately as Kasabach-Merritt Syndrome. This entry is the tumour itself, with or without that complication. It is related to tufted angioma, and the two may be one spectrum.

Mappings

MONDO
MONDO:0011927 tufted angioma Not Yet Curated
skos:relatedMatch manual curation
MONDO keeps tufted angioma as a class of its own, under skin hemangioma. The sources read the two tumours either as one neoplastic spectrum or as two related diseases (the hypotheses tufted_angioma_one_spectrum and tufted_angioma_two_diseases, and the discussion on them). On the spectrum reading they are two forms of one neoplasm, of which this entry covers the KHE form, even if, as one cited series reports, the WHO classification has combined them; on the other they are separate diseases. Either way neither class is recorded as narrower, and tufted angioma is mapped as related rather than added as a subtype.

3
A somatic activating GNA14 variant drives the growth of the tumour's endothelium
gna14_activation EMERGING
Evidence balance 2 support 1 refute
Reported in one KHE in the 2016 discovery study, in which the mutant made cultured endothelial cells and melanocytes growth-factor independent through MAPK; a later series found no GNA14 mutation in five further KHEs, and the 2020 review leaves open whether such mutations cause the tumour or arise later in it. The causal edge from the GNA14 node opts in to this hypothesis.

Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma are one neoplasm at two ends of a spectrum
tufted_angioma_one_spectrum CANONICAL
Evidence balance 14 support
The 2020 review treats KHE and tufted angioma as one neoplastic spectrum, the two able to occur in the same biopsy specimen of one patient, and the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon is defined as arising only with these two tumours. A 2026 series reads the WHO classification of soft tissue and bone tumours as suggesting they may be different manifestations or stages of one tumour, and an eight-case series (2021) reports that the WHO soft tissue classification has now combined the two. A methylation study of 7 KHE and 3 tufted angiomas found a common pattern, separate from that of vascular malformations, which its authors read as further evidence that the two potentially form one entity. The two share an endothelial immunophenotype, which a PROX1 study read as support for the two being closely related, if not identical; a 2003 report described one patient's tumour changing between the two, and a 2023 letter described tufted angioma appearing where a KHE with the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, diagnosed from laboratory tests and MRI with no biopsy reported, had been. A 2022 review of the literature found that four of five comparative studies of the pair from 2019 to 2022 considered them one spectrum, and remarked that different names are used for the same histomorphology depending on where the lesion lies. This is a question of classification; no causal edge in the entry opts in to it.

Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma are two related but separate diseases
tufted_angioma_two_diseases ALTERNATIVE
Evidence balance 8 support 1 refute
A 2003 report notes that the classification of vascular tumours then in use kept the two as separate disease entities, MONDO keeps separate classes, and one of five comparative studies of the pair from 2019 to 2022 treated them as different entities. The sources describe tufted angioma as a benign or intermediate skin lesion and KHE as locally aggressive, an eight-case series (2021) treats tufted angioma as a benign tumour to tell KHE apart from, a 2022 review says they differ mainly in location and behaviour, a 2026 series describes tufted angioma as typically discrete tufts of capillaries against an infiltrative lobular growth in KHE, and in a 2019 imaging comparison KHE was more likely to be thick, ill-defined, richly vascular and hard. These differences fit two ends of one spectrum as well, so they do not decide between the readings. The current WHO classification, as two cited series describe it, suggests the two may be manifestations or stages of one tumour, or has combined them. This is a question of classification; no causal edge in the entry opts in to it.

Discussions and Knowledge Gaps

1
Are kaposiform haemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma one neoplasm at two ends of a spectrum, or two related diseases?
CONTROVERSY OPEN khe_tufted_angioma_one_spectrum_or_two
Attached to
mechanistic_hypotheses#tufted_angioma_one_spectrum mechanistic_hypotheses#tufted_angioma_two_diseases
The 2020 review treats the two as one spectrum, a methylation study reads them as potentially one entity, and four of five comparative studies from 2019 to 2022 (which may include some of these), counted by a 2022 review of the literature, considered them one spectrum; a 2003 report described one patient's tumour changing between them, a 2023 letter described tufted angioma appearing where a KHE had been, and the WHO classification, as two cited series describe it, suggests they may be manifestations or stages of one tumour, or has combined them. The same 2003 report notes that the classification then in use kept them as separate entities, one study in the 2022 review treats them as different, and the sources describe differences in location, behaviour, histology and imaging that fit either reading. MONDO keeps separate classes, and this entry maps tufted angioma as a related match rather than a subtype. Which reading holds bears on whether findings, risks and treatment results reported for one tumour, or for series that pool both, can be carried over to the other.

Pathophysiology

4
Somatic GNA14 Activation
The cause of most tumours is unknown. A somatic activating GNA14 variant (c.614A>T, p.Gln205Leu) was found in one KHE in the 2016 discovery study, a finding the 2020 review gives as 1/3 of KHE specimens; a later sequencing series of five KHEs and two tufted angiomas found none. The mutations reported in KHE are sporadic, not germline. GNA14 belongs to the GNAQ family, whose G alpha subunits bind G-protein-coupled receptors. No cited source establishes the cell in which the variant arises within the tumour, so no cell is bound here. The node covers only tumours carrying the variant (one KHE in the cited studies), and even there the review leaves open whether it is a cause or a later change in the tumour.
A somatic activating GNA14 variant drives the growth of the tumour's endothelium

Lymphatic-Type Endothelial Proliferation
The tumour grows as infiltrating nodules of spindled endothelial cells lining slit-like or crescentic vessels. The endothelium stains for CD31 and CD34 and for the lymphatic markers LYVE1, PROX1 and podoplanin (D2-40), and not for GLUT-1. Angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis are dysregulated and progressive. How fast the endothelium proliferates is not settled: the cohort of 70 reports Ki-67 on the endothelial cells, while in the lesion the 2020 review illustrates only a few nuclei stained for it. The 2020 review adds VEGFR-3 to these lymphatic markers; in a thoracic series of 7 KHEs and 6 kaposiform lymphangiomatoses, all lesions examined had spindle tumour cells staining for CD31 and D2-40, and CD31-positive cells isolated from three of six patients' tumours carried CD31, Ki-67 and LYVE1 in culture. Which signals drive the programme is not established. The review suggests, from the expression of both in KHE, that the VEGF-C/VEGFR3 axis may contribute to the tumour's aggressive behaviour, while serum VEGF-C was lower in KHE patients with the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, a different compartment from the tissue, against a comparison group the abstract does not state. Serum angiopoietin-2 was 14-fold raised in KHE when the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon was present and not when it was absent, and the serum study proposes it, with the angiopoietin-1 that was lower alongside VEGF-C, as a marker of the phenomenon's coagulopathy. The review offers vascular remodelling, such as vessel sprouting and inflammatory lymphangiogenesis, as a possible explanation of the rise, raises the possibility of a paracrine effect on the tumour's endothelial cells, and also raises the possibility of a role for angiopoietin-2 in the phenomenon itself.

Locally Infiltrative Tumour Growth
An intermediate, locally aggressive tumour without distant metastasis. In a cohort of 70 children, 85% had lesions deep into multiple muscles and MRI showed bone destruction in 34%; in a series of 64 patients, 44% had enhancing, infiltrative soft-tissue thickening. The growth produces the mass, the pain, the joint involvement and the bone destruction. Infiltration into muscle or deeper, and a retroperitoneal or intrathoracic site, are associated with a higher likelihood of the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon. Loss of motion in nearby large joints may follow, by a route that is uncertain.
Downstream
Locally Aggressive Cutaneous Mass In most patients the infiltrating tumour presents as a soft-tissue mass with skin findings.
Pain Pain can come from the infiltrating, destructive growth.
Joint Involvement The infiltrating tumour invades the joints near it.
Limited Joint Range of Motion In a cohort selected for loss of joint motion, most limb lesions were on or next to large joints. The cohort calls the cause uncertain and, citing earlier work, states that infiltration of muscle, connective tissue and joint structures can lead to fibrosis and contracture.
Bone Destruction The tumour invades and destroys bone.
Chronic Lymphedema Lymphoedema can follow the tumour, more often when it is large (10 cm or more), mixed and in a limb. On lymphoscintigraphy of 25 patients, 24 of them with a limb tumour, lymphatic stasis within the involved lesion was found in all 22 with abnormal findings, and lymphoedema was on the side of the lesion, as it was in all 13 affected patients of the cohort of 118. The 2020 review suggests that a tumour of the proximal limb, particularly at or near the inguinal or axillary lymph nodes, may influence lymphatic development or damage the lymphatic vessels, and reports a hypothesis that, for such tumours, obstruction of lymphatic flow during the acute Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon may lead to lymphoedema; it adds that inflammation may also play a role. In the cohort of 118, of whom 13 had lymphoedema, a history of the phenomenon and sirolimus treatment were not significant predictors of lymphoedema; with 13 cases this does not exclude them. The lymphoscintigraphy series' abstract names no centre, so whether it shares patients with the cohort of 118 is not known.
Intralesional Platelet Trapping The tumour vasculature traps platelets. In 107 referrals, infiltration into muscle or deeper, and a retroperitoneal or intrathoracic site, were associated with a higher likelihood of the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon. In a series of 146 patients, mixed lesions (a cutaneous lesion with deep infiltration) had about four times the odds of the phenomenon that superficial ones had, in the univariate analysis.

Intralesional Platelet Trapping
Platelets are trapped inside the tumour vasculature, which is seen histologically with or without the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon. In the phenomenon the trapped platelets are activated and aggregate, the coagulation cascade is activated and clotting factors are consumed, with profound thrombocytopenia. Curated separately as Kasabach-Merritt Syndrome, which holds the mechanism, its treatment and its trials; this step only hands over to that entry.

Histopathology

7
Infiltrating Vascular Nodules
The histological hallmark in the review: infiltrating, defined, rounded and confluent nodules of spindle endothelial cells. The 33-case series describes irregular, infiltrating nodules of compressed vessels that in places resemble a capillary haemangioma and in others Kaposi sarcoma; in three adult cases densely packed spindle cells grew in a lobular or nodular pattern, closely associated with small slit-like and sieve-like vessels; and in most of eight cases nodular growth predominated over a minor spindle-cell component, with the nodules of tumours in the extremities infiltrating dermis and subcutaneous fat. In a thoracic series of 7 KHE and 6 kaposiform lymphangiomatosis patients, the nodules of KHE were more defined and confluent than the sparse, poorly marginated spindle-cell clusters of kaposiform lymphangiomatosis.

Glomeruloid Islands with Pericytes and Fibrin Thrombi
Scattered "epithelioid" or glomeruloid islands of endothelium with clusters of plump actin-positive pericytes, stippled haemosiderin and CD61-positive fibrin thrombi, which the 33-case series takes to be the likely sites where platelets are consumed; the eight-case series' introduction describes the nodules as glomeruloid aggregates of vascular channels with a surrounding pericytic layer. The abstract on three adult cases describes small nodules of plumper, epithelioid tumour cells in one lesion, and well-formed capillaries frequently containing fibrin thrombi mainly at the periphery of the nodules, without calling either glomeruloid.

Lymphatic Channels Within and Around the Tumour
Lymphatic channels are found within and around the tumour. The review describes the spindle cells as aligning into malformed lymphatic channels; the 33-case series found small and large lymphatic channels in 22 of 33 cases, typically at the periphery of or deep to the main mass; and in the eight-case series lymphangioma-like vessels were recorded in 4 of 8 tumours (its Table 2), and one case had prominent lymphatic vessels around the nodules. One of three adult cases had an associated lymphangiomatosis of the dermis and subcutis.

Vascular Endothelial Markers
The endothelium of the nodules stains for the vascular endothelial markers CD31 and CD34 and for FLI1 in the 33-case series, and the endothelial cells for CD31, CD34 and ERG in the eight-case series, with smooth-muscle-actin-positive pericytes around the lumina. Lymphatic Endothelial Markers
Lymphatic markers are expressed too, though not in every compartment. The review lists podoplanin (D2-40), PROX1, LYVE-1 and VEGFR-3 in the lesional endothelium. A 314-tumour survey found a prominent PROX1-positive endothelial component in all 5 KHE it examined, with the spindle cells of the pericytic population PROX1-negative, and podoplanin in the 3 it examined further; the eight-case series' discussion places D2-40, LYVE-1 and VEGFR3, markers that series did not test itself, in the zones of lymphatic channels beside the glomeruloid areas; and in a thoracic series of 7 KHE and 6 kaposiform lymphangiomatosis patients every lesion examined had CD31- and D2-40-positive spindle cells. A study of 18 KHE among 75 vascular lesions found that tufted angioma shares KHE's endothelial immunophenotype, and found PROX1 helpful in distinguishing KHE from infantile haemangioma and pyogenic granuloma, which lacked it. PROX1 is not specific to KHE: the 314-tumour survey found it also in lymphangiomas, spindle cell and venous haemangiomas, retiform haemangioendothelioma and Kaposi sarcoma.

Medical Actions

8
Sirolimus
Action: PharmacotherapyNCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment is this clinical intervention This treatment is Pharmacotherapy (NCIT:C15986). NCIT:C15986 is a clinical intervention from the NCI Thesaurus. NCIT:C15986
Agent: sirolimus CHEBI:9168 Chemical Entities of Biological Interest (CHEBI) Relation: this treatment uses this therapeutic agent This treatment uses sirolimus (CHEBI:9168). CHEBI:9168 is a therapeutic agent from Chemical Entities of Biological Interest.
Platform: Small molecule
Dosing: twice a day every 0.5 days
An mTOR inhibitor. In a randomised trial in KHE with the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, in which sirolimus was given for at least 12 months, adding a short course of prednisolone raised the week-4 platelet response from 24 of 36 to 35 of 37; in a randomised trial in KHE without the phenomenon, low-dose sirolimus was non-inferior to high-dose at one year (about 90% response in both); in a cohort of 167 patients, 92.2% had a durable response. On dose, a series of 21 patients, started on sirolimus alone at 0.8 mg/m2 twice a day once there was no sign of the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon aiming for a trough of 5 to 20 ng/mL, found faster tumour shrinkage above a trough of 10 ng/mL and no further gain above 15, in groups of 8, 7 and 6 patients; the randomised trial in KHE without the phenomenon found a trough of 5 to 8 ng/mL non-inferior to 10 to 15 for a volume reduction of at least 20% at month 12, with similar total and serious adverse events but fewer respiratory, skin and mucosal ones. In a pharmacokinetic model of 17 children aged 0.2 to 6 years, the drug's apparent clearance rose with age and was higher in boys than in girls of the same age, which the authors put down to body weight. In the patients with the phenomenon in a 52-patient series, tumour shrinkage did not differ significantly between the 21 given short-term prednisolone for severe symptoms and those on sirolimus alone, whereas the randomised prednisolone trial in KHE with the phenomenon reported better objective lesion responses at month 12 with it. On stopping, rebound growth followed discontinuation in 17.3% of the patients of the cohort of 167 who stopped sirolimus (the abstract does not say how many stopped), associated with early discontinuation and with mixed lesion type, for which the abstract's own confidence interval includes 1; in a series of 26, 25 of them with the phenomenon, 20 completed a course of 28.3 months on average, and the series had no recurrence over a median follow-up of 32 months (the abstract does not say whether follow-up ran from the start or the end of treatment). In the cohort of 167, nonresponse, relapse and long-term sequelae remained despite intensified and prolonged treatment. On harms, serious adverse events were most common in the first year and long-term treatment brought no unacceptable cumulative toxicity in that cohort; in the randomised prednisolone trial, total and grade 3-4 adverse events were similar with and without prednisolone; no patient in the 52-patient series stopped permanently for toxicity, and the 26-patient series reported mild side effects; and a 4-month-old on sirolimus and a prednisolone taper developed Pneumocystis pneumonia with respiratory failure needing extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, after which the authors advise considering prophylaxis.
Mechanism Target:
INHIBITS Lymphatic-Type Endothelial Proliferation — Aimed at the growth of the tumour's endothelium. How sirolimus acts in KHE is not settled. A 2025 review lists possible effects on platelet activation, inflammation, angiogenesis, lymphangiogenesis and fibrosis, of which the antiangiogenic and antilymphangiogenic effects bear on this node, and the 2020 review places it beside antilymphatic strategies. Serum angiopoietin-2 fell after 12 months of treatment in kaposiform lymphangiomatosis and in KHE with the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, reported together in the abstract, with most patients responding, which may track the phenomenon rather than the endothelium; and sirolimus downregulated ATG9B in endothelial cells cultured from patients' tumours, a preliminary transcriptome finding.

Action: PharmacotherapyNCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment is this clinical intervention This treatment is Pharmacotherapy (NCIT:C15986). NCIT:C15986 is a clinical intervention from the NCI Thesaurus. NCIT:C15986
Agent: corticosteroid CHEBI:50858 Chemical Entities of Biological Interest (CHEBI) Relation: this treatment uses this therapeutic agent This treatment uses corticosteroid (CHEBI:50858). CHEBI:50858 is a therapeutic agent from Chemical Entities of Biological Interest.
Platform: Small molecule
Recommended as a first-line treatment of the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon because they raise the platelet count quickly; given alone, many cases do not improve, with response rates of 10 to 27%. The 2020 review gives oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg a day or intravenous methylprednisolone 1.6 mg/kg a day, and recommends them for the severe Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon together with vincristine or sirolimus. One cohort's discussion describes starting methylprednisolone at 2 to 3 mg/kg a day for less than a week, and says 5 to 6 mg/kg a day can be used for extremely low platelet counts and life-threatening conditions; its results report giving every child with the phenomenon who was operated on high-dose methylprednisolone (5 to 6 mg/kg a day), a haemostatic or immunoglobulin before surgery, and its abstract says 89% of those operated on had high-dose methylprednisolone beforehand. Prednisolone is also the add-on in the randomised trial of sirolimus. The review notes that the 2013 consensus recommendations of corticosteroids, vincristine or both rest on expert opinion rather than rigorous clinical studies. Long-term use brings temporary growth retardation, a higher risk of infection and behavioural change, and the 21-child series, citing earlier work, adds hypertension, sleep disturbance and hyperglycaemia; so the review advises weaning them as soon as medically feasible, and the VASCERN-VASCA pathway tapering and stopping them once the phenomenon has resolved and the child is stable.
Mechanism Target:
MODULATES Intralesional Platelet Trapping — Used to raise the platelet count in the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon; how they act on the trapping is not described in the cited sources.

Vincristine
Action: PharmacotherapyNCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment is this clinical intervention This treatment is Pharmacotherapy (NCIT:C15986). NCIT:C15986 is a clinical intervention from the NCI Thesaurus. NCIT:C15986
Agent: vincristine CHEBI:28445 Chemical Entities of Biological Interest (CHEBI) Relation: this treatment uses this therapeutic agent This treatment uses vincristine (CHEBI:28445). CHEBI:28445 is a therapeutic agent from Chemical Entities of Biological Interest.
Platform: Small molecule
Dosing: once weekly every 7 days
A vinca alkaloid, given intravenously at 0.05 mg/kg once a week in the 2020 review's table, through a central line. Consensus-derived guidelines recommended vincristine, with or without corticosteroids, as first-line treatment of KHE with the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, and the review notes that the 2013 consensus recommendations of corticosteroids, vincristine or both rest on expert opinion rather than rigorous clinical studies; the review now considers sirolimus with corticosteroids a first-line therapy (versus vincristine with corticosteroids); many clinicians and families prefer sirolimus because vincristine needs a central line; and a 21-child series says sirolimus has superseded it in many centres. The VASCERN-VASCA pathway adds vincristine when a lesion compresses vital structures or lies in a life-threatening site, or when sirolimus and corticosteroids fail; notes that, once the diagnosis has been re-confirmed, adding it can shrink a tumour without the phenomenon that has not responded; and allows stopping it once the lesion no longer shrinks. First-line vincristine has an overall response rate of 72%; in a multicentre cohort that pools KHE with tufted angioma, its radiological response at three months was higher than sirolimus's, with no difference at six. In the single-centre series of 21 children, 16 were treated with vincristine, weekly for 6 to 12 weeks and then less often, for a median total of 185 days: 11 needed no other treatment, 3 moved on to sirolimus, and there were no recurrences over a median follow-up of 6.1 years; the series acknowledges an institutional preference for vincristine. The review cites mounting evidence that vincristine alone fails in very severe disease, while in that series the 3 children with the severe Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon who began vincristine had the phenomenon resolve after two doses, alongside supportive measures; one of them later moved to sirolimus. Complications there were common but, in the authors' words, mild in most: 15 of 16 had at least one, 13 were admitted with a febrile illness, 8 had what the authors call bone marrow suppression (a haemoglobin below 100 g/L, managed with iron), 6 had poor weight gain or growth, one of them admitted for tube feeding, 3 central lines were removed early, and 2 children had possible neuropathy, a transient ptosis. Another cohort, citing earlier work, says vincristine is given to children with the phenomenon who do not respond to corticosteroids, but is not used routinely because of its complications, among them myelosuppression in neonates, peripheral neuropathy, constipation and intestinal obstruction.
Mechanism Target:
INHIBITS Lymphatic-Type Endothelial Proliferation — Aimed at the growth of the tumour.

Surgical resection
Action: tumour resectionNCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment is this clinical intervention This treatment is tumour resection, annotated with Tumor Resection (NCIT:C164212). NCIT:C164212 is a clinical intervention from the NCI Thesaurus. Ontology label: Tumor Resection NCIT:C164212
Platform: Surgery
Complete resection is an option where it can be done safely, but surgery is rarely an option for extensive tumours or where it would badly impair function. The VASCERN-VASCA pathway says radical surgery that avoids functional defects and mutilation can be curative for the rare small tumour without the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, and after failed medical treatment reserves surgery for the rare tumours that can be removed completely without mutilation. Elective resection during the active phenomenon is ill advised: these young children, with very vascular tumours, are at higher risk of blood loss, iatrogenic injury and a worse coagulopathy. The review also cites evidence that manipulating the tumour, by surgery or trauma, can set off the phenomenon, whether or not the child has had it before. Surgery can also remove a fibrofatty residuum or reconstruct damaged structures. Both cited series nonetheless operated on children with the phenomenon. In one single-centre cohort, where over 90% were operated on, the authors favoured early surgery; all 8 low-risk patients recovered after surgery without recurrence, and 6 cases (9%) recurred after a few months as small lesions. In a single-centre series of 21 children, 6 tumours were excised, and the phenomenon resolved within 24 hours of the operation in the 2 of them with the severe Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon.
Mechanism Target:
INHIBITS Locally Infiltrative Tumour Growth — Removes the tumour where a complete and safe resection is possible.

Transarterial embolisation
Action: transarterial embolisationNCI Thesaurus (NCIT) Relation: this treatment is this clinical intervention This treatment is transarterial embolisation, annotated with Arterial Embolization (NCIT:C15917). NCIT:C15917 is a clinical intervention from the NCI Thesaurus. Ontology label: Arterial Embolization NCIT:C15917
Platform: Surgery
Arterial embolisation can at first reduce blood flow from the tumour and the risk of high-output cardiac failure, and may have a role in controlling the disease in children with the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon. It is technically difficult, since the feeding vessels in these young children are very small, and as an invasive procedure it may worsen the blood counts. The VASCERN-VASCA pathway keeps it, with surgery, for when medical treatment fails, recommends that referral centres do it, notes that in selected cases combining it with medical treatment can stabilise the child, and that embolising before surgery may shrink the tumour for a time and reduce bleeding at operation.
Mechanism Target:
MODULATES Locally Infiltrative Tumour Growth — Before surgery, may shrink the tumour for a time.

Diagnosis

2
Magnetic resonance imaging
Generally the first-line assessment, because the tumour's deep infiltration may not be apparent on examination or ultrasound. The lesion has ill-defined margins and crosses tissue planes, enhances diffusely, and is hypo- or iso-intense to muscle on T1 and hyperintense on T2.

Biopsy with immunohistochemistry
Biopsy is the reference standard and shows the lymphatic-type endothelium, but it is often not possible or not advised in severe Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon. The diagnosis integrates the clinical, imaging, haematological and histological features, and even with all of them it can be unclear.

Imaging Findings

7
Ill-Defined Infiltrative Mass
On MRI, KHE usually has ill-defined margins, crosses tissue planes and shows diffuse enhancement with adjacent fat stranding in unusual locations. The 2020 review calls MRI the usual first-line study because deep infiltration may not be apparent on examination or ultrasound, while the authors of a 2023 series call ultrasound the first choice for assessing KHE but note that it cannot clearly show the infiltrating part. In a series of 12 children studied by CT or MRI, 8 of the 10 tumours with images were locally invasive and involved two or more adjacent organs, 7 were infiltrative and 3 were well-defined solid masses. In a 64-patient MRI series, 28 (43.8%) had enhancing, infiltrative soft-tissue thickening, and ill-defined infiltrative lesions were more likely before 6 months of age. Against this, a 2023 comparison table gives well-defined margins on MRI for rapidly involuting congenital haemangioma, and a 2023 series, citing earlier work, describes infantile haemangioma on MRI as regular and well defined, without significant destruction of adjacent bone.

T2 Hyperintense Signal
On MRI, KHE is hyperintense to muscle on T2-weighted images. In a 64-patient series every lesion was also hypo- or isointense on T1-weighted images, and the 2020 review describes isointensity on T1. T2 hyperintensity was found in all 9 imaged by MRI in a 12-patient series (heterogeneously, with nearly isointense regions in four) and in all 4 imaged by MRI in a 2023 series of 27 infants (unevenly); the 12-patient abstract and the 2023 series give no T1 signal. A 2018 series of 25, with 22 imaged by MRI, differs on T1, with 15 isointense and 7 slightly hyperintense, and found heterogeneous or slightly hyperintense T2 signal with speckled hypointense foci in 17 (77%), which its authors call a feature unique to KHE.

Heterogeneous Contrast Enhancement
After contrast, KHE enhances heterogeneously in most reports: heterogeneously and intensely in 8 of the 10 tumours with CT or MRI in a 12-patient series (mildly in one), heterogeneously in 1 of the 2 with contrast MRI in a 2023 series, and diffusely and heterogeneously more often than tufted angioma among the 50 with MRI in a 2019 comparison; the 2023 authors, citing earlier work, note that most infantile haemangiomas enhance homogeneously with clear boundaries. In a 2018 series of 25, enhancement was notable in 15 and moderate in 3 of the 18 with contrast MRI, and feeding or draining vessels, seen as flow voids on T2 or linear enhancing vessels on enhanced CT or MRI, were found in 15. Signal voids are reported in 2 patients of the 12-patient series (9 had MRI), whose authors call them infrequent, flow voids in 2 of the 4 with MRI in the 2023 series, and as occasional in a 2023 comparison table. MRI with and without gadolinium also defines the extent of involvement and the response to treatment.

Heterogeneous Echogenicity on Ultrasound
Ultrasound is the modality of choice for small, superficial lesions. KHE is heterogeneous in echogenicity, with striated hypoechoic bands in some, and usually richly vascular (abundant or patchy flow in the 2023 series), though its overall echogenicity varies: in a 2023 series of 27 infants, the masses seen were moderately echoic in 13, hypoechoic in 9 and hyperechoic in 4 (one infant had no mass on ultrasound), and in a 2019 comparison of 40 KHE and 21 tufted angiomas, KHE was more likely than tufted angioma to be hypoechoic. In that comparison, 96.15% of KHE (no denominator given) had mixed echogenicity, against hyperechoic lesions in 42.9% of tufted angiomas, every KHE had ill-defined margins, and 3-D colour Doppler showed branch-shaped flow. In a 2018 series, in which 15 children had ultrasound, the masses were inhomogeneous and rich in vascularity. Ultrasound alone may not separate KHE from infantile haemangioma, as both look hypervascular; a 2023 comparison table lists heterogeneous echogenicity, ill-defined margins and an infiltrative pattern for KHE against an echogenic, well-defined mass for rapidly involuting congenital haemangioma.

Bone Destruction or Remodelling
The 2020 review calls bone and joint changes next to the tumour common: destruction of the adjacent cortex, injury of the epiphyseal region and invasion of nearby joints. Destructive changes or remodelling of adjacent bone were among the most common presenting features in a 64-patient MRI series, in 42.2%, more often from 6 months of age, and MRI showed bone destruction in 24 (34%) of a 70-patient series (how many had MRI is not stated), the ribs most often. In other series: bone changes in 4 patients of a 12-patient series (10 had CT or MRI findings), whose authors call them infrequent; reported with the CT findings of a 2018 series (13 with CT), ill-defined osteolytic destruction in one patient and erosion or remodelling of adjacent bone in three; and in a 2023 series, bone invasion in 3 of the 12 with CT and bone changes in 1 of the 4 with MRI. The 2018 authors call CT useful for showing osteolytic destruction, erosion and remodelling, and the 2023 authors, citing them, say CT shows these better. In a separate series of 12 children whose KHE was confined to bone on first imaging, two patterns appeared: a permeative or moth-eaten osteolytic pattern in 7, which the authors describe as involving epiphysis and metaphysis, one of the 7 with both patterns; and well-defined, saucer-like cortical excavation in 5, mainly of the metaphysis (4 of 5; one epiphyseal); none of the 12 had a significant periosteal reaction.

Diffusion on Diffusion-Weighted MRI
The two series that report diffusion-weighted imaging differ. In the 2018 series, the 5 masses imaged showed slightly restricted diffusion, with a mean apparent diffusion coefficient of 1.28 × 10⁻³ mm²/s; its authors say a low apparent diffusion coefficient helps distinguish KHE from infantile haemangioma (the series imaged no haemangiomas), and that the value of diffusion imaging in diagnosis needs testing in larger cohorts. In the 2023 series, the KHE imaged by MRI (4 of 27 infants; how many had diffusion imaging is not stated) showed no significant diffusion restriction.

Progression

3
Onset
Mostly in infancy: onset in infancy in 93% of 107 patients in one series, and as newborns in 60%.
Show evidence (1 reference)
PMID:22871490 SUPPORT DIRECT PRIMARY RESULT Human clinical
"KHE manifested in infancy in 93% of cases, with 60% as neonates."
Onset in infancy in 93% of 107.
Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon
Usually early. In a series of 146 patients, which defined the phenomenon as a platelet count below 100 × 10^9/L, it developed in 102 (69.9%), from the first day of life to 60 months of age (median 1 month). It was present at birth in 39.2% of those 102 and began within the first 6 months of age in 91.2%, after 1 year of age in four; 48.0% had no sign of it when the lesion was first assessed and developed it a median 1.25 months later, and in four, all with deep lesions, it was noted before a tumour mass was identified. In 107 referrals, 71% developed it, 11% after initial presentation. In 70 children in a 2024 series, which defined it from platelet counts and coagulation indices, 78% did, with thrombocytopenia starting at a median of 27.8 days of age, though that series' own counts by depth stage add up to 48 of the 70. The 107-referral series (2013) gives no definition in its abstract, so the three rates are not strictly comparable. Which tumours develop it: in the 146-patient series, a younger age at which the lesion was discovered, its size and a mixed lesion (a cutaneous lesion with deep infiltration into muscle, bone, intrathoracic or retroperitoneal sites) remained associated with it after adjustment (odds ratios 11.9, 5.08 and 2.96), while a trunk site was associated only before adjustment (87% against 59% at other sites, odds ratio 4.70), and head-neck and extremity lesions less often had it. Before adjustment, lesions discovered before 6 months of age had higher odds than those discovered at 12 months or later (odds ratio 59, 95% confidence interval 7.38 to 472; 1 of the 15 discovered at 12 months or later had it); lesions of 5 to 8 cm and of 8 cm or more had odds ratios of 6.8 and 14.2 against those under 5 cm (the phenomenon in 71% and 83%, against 26% under 5 cm); and mixed lesions had about four times the odds of the phenomenon that superficial ones had (80% against 50%). Deep, noncutaneous lesions as a group were not a significant factor (10 of 18 had it). By site, every lesion involving the mediastinum or the peritoneal cavity had it (three of the deep lesions were in the peritoneal cavity; the number involving the mediastinum is not given), as did 7 of 9 with retroperitoneal involvement (the authors, citing an earlier report, suggest that small retroperitoneal lesions without the phenomenon might go undetected), while none of the six confined to bone, joint and muscle did. The authors suggest those six may be physically constrained from expansion, and note that they tended to be more focal and smaller than mixed lesions. In the 107 referrals, a tumour infiltrating muscle or deeper was "6.3-fold more likely" to show it, and a retroperitoneal or intrathoracic site "18-fold higher", against a superficial tumour (the abstract does not say whether these are odds ratios); retroperitoneal and intrathoracic tumours had it in 85% and 100%; and tumours limited to bone or presenting after infancy did not. A 2020 review, which shares authors with the 146-patient series, puts the risk highest for congenital tumours of large size, especially over 8 cm. Among its limitations the 146-patient series names its retrospective design, the treatment of several congenital lesions that had no sign of the phenomenon at referral and might otherwise have developed it, and possible referral bias. The phenomenon itself is curated separately as Kasabach-Merritt Syndrome.

Outcome
The tumour can persist: about 17.4% of 167 patients on long-term sirolimus still had active disease or changed body structures at last follow-up, and in a cohort of 70 children all five treated without surgery (medicines, with or without sclerotherapy) were alive with tumour. Untreated tumour becomes progressively fibrotic, and some patients develop contractures and chronic pain; quality of life is lower than in healthy children. Deaths are few in recent cohorts: 2 of 70 in one, 2 of 159 (KHE and tufted angioma together) in another. Citing earlier studies, the 2018 musculoskeletal cohort states that in most patients the lesion is still present after long-term treatment and that residual lesions become progressively fibrotic; in that cohort, decreased joint motion appeared in one patient after sirolimus was tapered and stopped at 18 months, and improved on further courses.

Differential Diagnoses

8

Conditions with similar clinical presentations that must be differentiated from Kaposiform Hemangioendothelioma:

Infantile Hemangioma MONDO:0011191
Overlapping Features One of the most important tumours to rule out. Infantile haemangioma grows dramatically at about 5.5 to 7.5 weeks of age, its endothelial cells usually stain for GLUT1, which KHE lacks, and it lacks KHE's rounded nodules and the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon. KHE can be misdiagnosed as infantile haemangioma, as in a 19-month-old with a leg tumour that involved bone.
Distinguishing Features
  • Usually GLUT1-positive; GLUT1 and Lewis Y antigen are its markers, absent from KHE nodules
  • No rounded nodules and no Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon

Congenital Hemangioma Not Yet Curated MONDO:0018715
Overlapping Features Arises in utero and is fully formed at birth, in rapidly involuting, partially involuting and non-involuting forms, and can look very like KHE in the newborn period. It does not grow progressively after birth, whereas KHE with the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon appears to grow and becomes engorged and purpuric. Mild consumption of clotting factors can occur, without bleeding, and tends to resolve within 1 to 2 weeks, but a rapidly involuting congenital haemangioma with profound, transient thrombocytopenia has been reported, and so have rapidly involuting ones with severe, life-threatening phenomenon. A 2014 report sets the rapidly involuting form apart from KHE and tufted angioma, which it names as associated with the phenomenon, while a 2023 case report puts it at under 10% of congenital haemangiomas against about 42% to 71% of KHE. On biopsy, both the rapidly involuting form and KHE are GLUT1-negative, but only KHE carries lymphatic markers.
Distinguishing Features
  • Present and fully formed at birth, with no progressive growth after birth
  • Coagulopathy, when it occurs, usually mild and self-limited
  • Rapidly involuting form negative for lymphatic markers, which KHE expresses

Tufted Angioma Not Yet Curated MONDO:0011927
Overlapping Features Occurs in the same young children, in the skin as red to purple plaques, and is, with KHE, one of the two tumours to which the 2020 review's definition of the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon is limited. On ultrasound most tufted angiomas are well defined, and they are shallower and less vascular than KHE; on histology they show cannonball-like clusters of capillaries in the dermis. Some authors place the two at the benign and aggressive ends of one histological spectrum, and a 2021 series says the WHO classification of soft-tissue tumours has combined them after a long debate.
Distinguishing Features
  • Well-defined margins on ultrasound in most; KHE margins are ill defined
  • Shallower and less vascular than KHE on ultrasound

Kaposiform Lymphangiomatosis Not Yet Curated MONDO:0018736
Overlapping Features A rare, complex lymphatic disorder with multifocal or diffuse lesions that often involves the mediastinum, lungs, abdomen and several bones and, like KHE, contains spindled tumour cells. In a 2014 series most patients presented in childhood with respiratory or bleeding problems, and skin involvement was rare; in a 2019 series of thoracic disease, respiratory symptoms, effusions, thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy were common to both, presentation came later (mean 26.7 against 4.1 months), and diffuse lung and extrathoracic lesions were seen only in kaposiform lymphangiomatosis. Its thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy overlap with the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon: the 2014 series found the thrombocytopenia generally less severe, while a 2020 review notes that in some patients it is as severe. On histology its spindle cells form sparse, poorly marginated clusters rather than KHE's defined nodules; a somatic NRAS p.Q61R variant found in it is absent in KHE; and in the 2019 thoracic series it responded less to medical treatment.
Distinguishing Features

  • Later presentation, mostly in childhood; skin involvement rare

  • Somatic NRAS p.Q61R, absent in KHE
  • More refractory to medical treatment

Venous Malformation
Overlapping Features Extensive venous malformations are slow-flow malformations present at birth whose localized intravascular coagulopathy has been misdiagnosed as Kasabach-Merritt syndrome. It raises D-dimer, as the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon also does. The sources differ on fibrinogen: a 2002 series of extensive limb disease and the 2020 review describe it as low, while a 2022 study found it reduced in 3 of 29 patients with venous malformations, two of them with signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation, and describes consumption of fibrinogen and platelets as what may follow when severe cases progress to it. Platelets are normal or only slightly decreased and no inflamed ecchymotic tumour is present; events such as sclerotherapy or surgery can convert the coagulopathy to disseminated intravascular coagulation. It comes from stasis in the malformed vessels rather than from platelet trapping in a tumour, is lifelong, and is treated differently.
Distinguishing Features
  • Platelets normal or only slightly low at baseline; raised D-dimer is shared with the phenomenon
  • No large ecchymotic and inflammatory tumour
  • Enlarged, irregular venous channels lined by flattened endothelium

Overlapping Features A rare malignant soft-tissue tumour that mostly occurs before 1 year of age and can grow and become highly vascular within weeks or months; it is frequently misdiagnosed as infantile haemangioma or KHE. One case was first thought to be KHE with the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, and review of its laboratory studies suggested that disseminated intravascular coagulation may have been more likely. In a 2019 case, first treated as haemangioma until tissue examination gave the diagnosis, the infant developed disseminated intravascular coagulopathy with bleeding into the tumour during chemotherapy; its authors say the mechanism of the coagulopathy in this tumour is not well understood, and suggest that a process like Kasabach-Merritt syndrome could underlie it, given the tumour's vascularity.

description: >-
  Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma (KHE) is a rare vascular tumour of infancy and early childhood, of
  intermediate type: locally aggressive, it infiltrates skin, fat, muscle and bone, without distant
  metastasis. Its endothelium carries lymphatic markers. The cause of most tumours is unknown; a
  somatic activating GNA14 variant has been reported in one KHE in the cited studies, and whether it
  causes the tumour is not known. Its best-known complication, the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, in
  which platelets are trapped and consumed inside the tumour, is reported in 42% to 78% of patients
  across the KHE series cited here (40% where tufted angioma is pooled in) and is curated separately
  as Kasabach-Merritt Syndrome. This entry is the tumour itself, with or without that complication.
  It is related to tufted angioma, and the two may be one spectrum.

      id: MONDO:0011927
      label: tufted angioma
    mapping_predicate: skos:relatedMatch
    mapping_source: manual curation
    mapping_justification: >-
      MONDO keeps tufted angioma as a class of its own, under skin hemangioma. The sources read the
      two tumours either as one neoplastic spectrum or as two related diseases (the hypotheses
      tufted_angioma_one_spectrum and tufted_angioma_two_diseases, and the discussion on them). On
      the spectrum reading they are two forms of one neoplasm, of which this entry covers the KHE
      form, even if, as one cited series reports, the WHO classification has combined them; on the
      other they are separate diseases. Either way neither class is recorded as narrower, and tufted
      angioma is mapped as related rather than added as a subtype.
pathophysiology:
- name: Somatic GNA14 Activation
  description: >-
    The cause of most tumours is unknown. A somatic activating GNA14 variant (c.614A>T, p.Gln205Leu)
    was found in one KHE in the 2016 discovery study, a finding the 2020 review gives as 1/3 of KHE
    specimens; a later sequencing series of five KHEs and two tufted angiomas found none. The
    mutations reported in KHE are sporadic, not germline. GNA14 belongs to the GNAQ family, whose G
    alpha subunits bind G-protein-coupled receptors. No cited source establishes the cell in which
    the variant arises within the tumour, so no cell is bound here. The node covers only tumours
    carrying the variant (one KHE in the cited studies), and even there the review leaves open
    whether it is a cause or a later change in the tumour.
  biological_scale: MOLECULAR
  genes:
  - preferred_term: GNA14
    term:
      id: hgnc:4382
      label: GNA14
  molecular_functions:
  - preferred_term: G protein-coupled receptor binding
    term:
      id: GO:0001664
      label: G protein-coupled receptor binding
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:27476652
    reference_title: >-
      GNA14 Somatic Mutation Causes Congenital and Sporadic Vascular Tumors by MAPK Activation.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      We found somatic activating GNA14 c.614A>T (p.Gln205Leu) mutations in one KHE, one TA, and one
      LCH and a GNA11 c.547C>T (p.Arg183Cys) mutation in two LCH lesions.
    explanation: >-
      The original report: a somatic activating GNA14 variant in one KHE (and in one tufted angioma
      and one lobular capillary haemangioma).
  - reference: PMID:32014025
    reference_title: >-
      Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma: current knowledge and future perspectives.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Remarkably, the somatic activating GNA14 c.614A > T (p.Gln205Leu) mutation was found in 1/3 of
      KHE specimens and in 1/4 of TA specimens, although these studies were weakened by small sample
      size
    explanation: >-
      The review's figure for the same finding, 1/3 of KHE specimens, with its own caveat on sample
      size.
  - reference: PMID:32014025
    reference_title: >-
      Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma: current knowledge and future perspectives.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      It is likely that the origin of KHE is multifactorial, with genetic factors being part of the
      contributing triggers, although the mutations in KHE tumor are sporadic rather than germline.
    explanation: >-
      The mutations found in KHE are sporadic rather than germline.
  - reference: PMID:32014025
    reference_title: >-
      Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma: current knowledge and future perspectives.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      In general, the etiology of KHE remains largely unknown.
    explanation: >-
      The cause of most tumours is unknown, which limits this node to the tumours carrying the
      variant.
  - reference: PMID:32014025
    reference_title: >-
      Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma: current knowledge and future perspectives.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: >-
      The GNAQ family encodes Gα subunits that form a heterotrimer with Gβ and Gγ subunits and bind
      G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs).
    explanation: >-
      What the GNAQ-family proteins do: G alpha subunits that bind G-protein-coupled receptors.
      INDIRECT: stated for the family, of which the review names GNA14 a paralogue.
  downstream:
  - target: Lymphatic-Type Endothelial Proliferation
    causal_link_type: INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES
    hypothesis_groups:
    - gna14_activation
    description: >-
      Expressed in cultured endothelial cells and melanocytes, the mutant made the cells independent
      of growth factors by upregulating MAPK signalling; the steps from there to the tumour's
      lymphatic-type endothelium are not established. A later series found no GNA14 mutation in five
      further KHEs, and the 2020 review leaves open whether such mutations cause the tumour.
    evidence:
    - reference: PMID:27476652
      reference_title: >-
        GNA14 Somatic Mutation Causes Congenital and Sporadic Vascular Tumors by MAPK Activation.
      supports: SUPPORT
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: IN_VITRO
      snippet: >-
        GNA14 and GNA11 mutations induced changes in cellular morphology and rendered cells
        growth-factor independent by upregulating the MAPK pathway.
      explanation: >-
        The mutant's effect in primary human endothelial cells and melanocytes. INDIRECT: shown in
        cultured cells, not in the tumour.
    - reference: PMID:31887709
      reference_title: >-
        Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma - (epi)genetic analysis including
        genome-wide methylation profiling.
      supports: REFUTE
      directness: INDIRECT
      quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
      evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
      snippet: >-
        Using next generation sequencing, heterogeneous mutations were found in a subset of cases
        (2/7) without the presence of GNA14 mutations, previously reported in KHE and TA.
      explanation: >-
        In five further KHEs and two tufted angiomas no GNA14 mutation was found, which counts
        against GNA14 as the general driver of KHE. INDIRECT: other tumours, not the one carrying
        the variant.
- name: Lymphatic-Type Endothelial Proliferation
  description: >-
    The tumour grows as infiltrating nodules of spindled endothelial cells lining slit-like or
    crescentic vessels. The endothelium stains for CD31 and CD34 and for the lymphatic markers
    LYVE1, PROX1 and podoplanin (D2-40), and not for GLUT-1. Angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis are
    dysregulated and progressive. How fast the endothelium proliferates is not settled: the cohort
    of 70 reports Ki-67 on the endothelial cells, while in the lesion the 2020 review illustrates
    only a few nuclei stained for it.
    The 2020 review adds VEGFR-3 to these lymphatic markers; in a thoracic series of 7 KHEs and 6
    kaposiform lymphangiomatoses, all lesions examined had spindle tumour cells staining for CD31
    and D2-40, and CD31-positive cells isolated from three of six patients' tumours carried CD31,
    Ki-67 and LYVE1 in culture. Which signals drive the programme is not established. The review
    suggests, from the expression of both in KHE, that the VEGF-C/VEGFR3 axis may contribute to the
    tumour's aggressive behaviour, while serum VEGF-C was lower in KHE patients with the
    Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, a different compartment from the tissue, against a comparison group
    the abstract does not state. Serum angiopoietin-2 was 14-fold raised in KHE when the
    Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon was present and not when it was absent, and the serum study proposes
    it, with the angiopoietin-1 that was lower alongside VEGF-C, as a marker of the phenomenon's
    coagulopathy. The review offers vascular remodelling, such as vessel sprouting and inflammatory
    lymphangiogenesis, as a possible explanation of the rise, raises the possibility of a paracrine
    effect on the tumour's endothelial cells, and also raises the possibility of a role for
    angiopoietin-2 in the phenomenon itself.
  biological_scale: TISSUE
  cell_types:
  - preferred_term: lymphatic endothelial cell
    term:
      id: CL:0002138
      label: endothelial cell of lymphatic vessel
  biological_processes:
  - preferred_term: lymphangiogenesis
    modifier: INCREASED
    term:
      id: GO:0001946
      label: lymphangiogenesis
  - preferred_term: angiogenesis
    modifier: INCREASED
    term:
      id: GO:0001525
      label: angiogenesis
  - preferred_term: endothelial cell proliferation
    modifier: INCREASED
    term:
      id: GO:0001935
      label: endothelial cell proliferation
  notes: >-
    Not conformed to the tumor_angiogenesis or mtorc1_hyperactivation modules. In KHE the
    endothelium is the tumour itself, whereas tumor_angiogenesis models vessels recruited by a
    tumour of another lineage; and no cited source reports, in its abstract or, where its full text
    is cached, its full text, loss of an mTORC1 regulator, or a measurement of mTOR pathway
    activity, in KHE, whereas mtorc1_hyperactivation begins with such a loss. The cited sources name
    sirolimus as an mTOR inhibitor. The 2020 review places mTOR in general signalling downstream of
    VEGFR-3, Tie-2 and G-protein-coupled receptors, and the platelet study's introduction (2023)
    says that variants in GNAQ-family genes and in PIK3CA reported in vascular tumours are
    supposedly associated with abnormal VEGF receptor activation and downstream PI3K/Akt/mTOR
    signalling in lymphatic endothelial cells, which trigger KHE growth; none measures mTOR activity
    in KHE.

  - reference: PMID:32014025
    reference_title: >-

- name: Locally Infiltrative Tumour Growth
  description: >-
    An intermediate, locally aggressive tumour without distant metastasis. In a cohort of 70
    children, 85% had lesions deep into multiple muscles and MRI showed bone destruction in 34%; in
    a series of 64 patients, 44% had enhancing, infiltrative soft-tissue thickening. The growth
    produces the mass, the pain, the joint involvement and the bone destruction. Infiltration into
    muscle or deeper, and a retroperitoneal or intrathoracic site, are associated with a higher
    likelihood of the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon.
    Loss of motion in nearby large joints may follow, by a route that is uncertain.
  biological_scale: TISSUE

  - reference: PMID:32014025

    explanation: >-
      The tumour is of intermediate type and locally aggressive.

- name: Intralesional Platelet Trapping
  description: >-
    Platelets are trapped inside the tumour vasculature, which is seen histologically with or
    without the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon. In the phenomenon the trapped platelets are activated
    and aggregate, the coagulation cascade is activated and clotting factors are consumed, with
    profound thrombocytopenia. Curated separately as Kasabach-Merritt Syndrome, which holds the
    mechanism, its treatment and its trials; this step only hands over to that entry.

mechanistic_hypotheses:
- hypothesis_group_id: gna14_activation
  hypothesis_label: >-
    A somatic activating GNA14 variant drives the growth of the tumour's endothelium
  status: EMERGING
  description: >-
    Reported in one KHE in the 2016 discovery study, in which the mutant made cultured endothelial
    cells and melanocytes growth-factor independent through MAPK; a later series found no GNA14
    mutation in five further KHEs, and the 2020 review leaves open whether such mutations cause the
    tumour or arise later in it. The causal edge from the GNA14 node opts in to this hypothesis.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:27476652
    reference_title: >-
      GNA14 Somatic Mutation Causes Congenital and Sporadic Vascular Tumors by MAPK Activation.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      We found somatic activating GNA14 c.614A>T (p.Gln205Leu) mutations in one KHE, one TA, and one
      LCH and a GNA11 c.547C>T (p.Arg183Cys) mutation in two LCH lesions.
    explanation: >-
      The variant in one KHE. INDIRECT: a finding in one tumour, not a causal role.
  - reference: PMID:27476652
    reference_title: >-
      GNA14 Somatic Mutation Causes Congenital and Sporadic Vascular Tumors by MAPK Activation.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: IN_VITRO
    snippet: >-
      GNA14 and GNA11 mutations induced changes in cellular morphology and rendered cells
      growth-factor independent by upregulating the MAPK pathway.
    explanation: >-
      The mutant's effect in primary human endothelial cells and melanocytes. INDIRECT: shown in
      cultured cells, not in the tumour.
  - reference: PMID:31887709

      genome-wide methylation profiling.
    supports: REFUTE
    directness: INDIRECT

    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-

      (2/7) without the presence of GNA14 mutations, previously reported in KHE and TA.
    explanation: >-
      No GNA14 mutation in five further KHEs and two tufted angiomas. INDIRECT: other tumours.
- hypothesis_group_id: tufted_angioma_one_spectrum
  hypothesis_label: >-
    Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma are one neoplasm at two ends of a spectrum
  status: CANONICAL
  description: >-
    The 2020 review treats KHE and tufted angioma as one neoplastic spectrum, the two able to occur
    in the same biopsy specimen of one patient, and the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon is defined as
    arising only with these two tumours. A 2026 series reads the WHO classification of soft tissue
    and bone tumours as suggesting they may be different manifestations or stages of one tumour, and
    an eight-case series (2021) reports that the WHO soft tissue classification has now combined the
    two. A methylation study of 7 KHE and 3 tufted angiomas found a common pattern, separate from
    that of vascular malformations, which its authors read as further evidence that the two
    potentially form one entity. The two share an endothelial immunophenotype, which a PROX1 study
    read as support for the two being closely related, if not identical; a 2003 report described one
    patient's tumour changing between the two, and a 2023 letter described tufted angioma appearing
    where a KHE with the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, diagnosed from laboratory tests and MRI with
    no biopsy reported, had been. A 2022 review of the literature found that four of five
    comparative studies of the pair from 2019 to 2022 considered them one spectrum, and remarked
    that different names are used for the same histomorphology depending on where the lesion lies.
    This is a question of classification; no causal edge in the entry opts in to it.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:32014025
    reference_title: >-
      Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma: current knowledge and future perspectives.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: >-
      Conceptually, KHE and TA are part of the same neoplastic spectrum and can be present in the
      same biopsy specimen of the same patient
    explanation: >-
      The review: one neoplastic spectrum, the two able to occur in the same biopsy specimen of one
      patient.

    snippet: >-

- hypothesis_group_id: tufted_angioma_two_diseases
  hypothesis_label: >-
    Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma are two related but separate diseases
  status: ALTERNATIVE
  description: >-
    A 2003 report notes that the classification of vascular tumours then in use kept the two as
    separate disease entities, MONDO keeps separate classes, and one of five comparative studies of
    the pair from 2019 to 2022 treated them as different entities. The sources describe tufted
    angioma as a benign or intermediate skin lesion and KHE as locally aggressive, an eight-case
    series (2021) treats tufted angioma as a benign tumour to tell KHE apart from, a 2022 review
    says they differ mainly in location and behaviour, a 2026 series describes tufted angioma as
    typically discrete tufts of capillaries against an infiltrative lobular growth in KHE, and in a
    2019 imaging comparison KHE was more likely to be thick, ill-defined, richly vascular and hard.
    These differences fit two ends of one spectrum as well, so they do not decide between the
    readings. The current WHO classification, as two cited series describe it, suggests the two may
    be manifestations or stages of one tumour, or has combined them. This is a question of
    classification; no causal edge in the entry opts in to it.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:12771476
    reference_title: >-
      Transformation between Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: >-
      Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma are viewed as two separate disease entities
      in the current classification of vascular tumors.
    explanation: >-
      In 2003, the classification of vascular tumours then in use kept the two as separate disease
      entities.
  - reference: PMID:31887709
    reference_title: >-
      Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma - (epi)genetic analysis including
      genome-wide methylation profiling.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma (KHE) is a locally aggressive vascular condition of childhood
      and is clinicopathologically related to tufted angioma (TA), a benign skin lesion.
    explanation: >-
      KHE locally aggressive, tufted angioma a benign skin lesion. INDIRECT: a difference in
      behaviour, which also fits two ends of one spectrum.
  - reference: PMID:36604299
    reference_title: >-
      Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma: two entities of the same
      clinicopathological spectrum.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: INDIRECT
    quote_role: BACKGROUND
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-

    explanation: >-

  - reference: PMID:31373042

    explanation: >-
      On imaging, KHE was more likely than tufted angioma to be thick, ill-defined, richly vascular
      and hard. INDIRECT: group differences that also fit one spectrum.
  - reference: PMID:41680958
    reference_title: >-
      Primary osseous kaposiform hemangioendothelioma confined to long bones: a retrospective

    supports: SUPPORT

    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL

phenotypes:
- category: Integumentary
  name: Locally Aggressive Cutaneous Mass
  description: >-
    In most patients the tumour presents as a mass with skin findings over it: an enlarging
    cutaneous lesion at presentation in 75% of 107 patients in one series, a blue-purple cutaneous
    mass in 89% of 70 children in another (64 of 70, 91%, in its results), and visible skin lesions
    in 90.6% of 64 patients in a third; 11% of the 107 had no skin findings. In the cohort of 70 the
    tumour lay most often in the lower limbs and trunk.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: locally aggressive cutaneous mass
    term:
      id: HP:0100742
      label: Vascular neoplasm
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:22871490

      107 referrals.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: PRIMARY_RESULT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Common presenting features included enlarging cutaneous lesion (75%), thrombocytopenia (56%),
      and musculoskeletal pain or decreased function (23%).
    explanation: >-
      An enlarging skin lesion at presentation in 75% of 107 patients.
  - reference: PMID:22871490

  name: Pain
  frequency: OCCASIONAL
  description: >-
    Musculoskeletal pain or reduced function at presentation in 23% of 107 patients in one series,
    and local pain or joint dysfunction in 20% of 70 in another (each series counts the two
    together); acute pain at the tumour is common during the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon. The
    frequency band rests on the two series' figures, which do not count pain during the phenomenon
    separately; it is not an estimate of that pain.

    motion, 12 had chronic pain, defined as daily pain for at least 3 months, including 4 of the 5
    whose lesions involved the spine.

- category: Musculoskeletal
  name: Limited Joint Range of Motion
  description: >-
    Decreased range of motion of joints near the tumour, defined as an extension loss of at least 10
    degrees, flexion under 120 degrees or both, can develop in KHE without the Kasabach-Merritt
    phenomenon. In a cohort of 29 such patients, selected because they had it and had never had the
    phenomenon, it appeared within 2 years of onset in 72.4%, while 8 did not have it at the first
    evaluation and developed it later, and only 2 had it before the age of 12 months. Of the 29
    lesions, 26 involved the limbs; of all 29, 10 were mixed-type lesions that infiltrated deeply
    into muscle, bone and joints and 17 were confined to the muscle, bone and joint regions; the
    knee was the joint most often involved, then the shoulder and hip. Decreased motion also
    occurred in several patients who attained partial tumour involution. The authors note that its
    cause is uncertain; citing earlier work, they state that tumour infiltration of muscle,
    connective tissue and joint structures can lead to diffuse muscle fibrosis and joint
    contracture. Because the cohort was selected for it, these figures are not a frequency in KHE.
  phenotype_term:
    preferred_term: decreased range of motion of joints near the tumour
    term:
      id: HP:0001376
      label: Limitation of joint mobility
  evidence:

      without Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon: clinical characteristics and management.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      Patients were included if they 1) had verified KHE by pathological examination; 2) showed
      decreased ROM; 3) had no history of KMP
    explanation: >-
      The cohort's selection: patients with decreased range of motion and no history of the
      Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, so its figures are not frequencies in KHE.
  - reference: PMID:30233248
    reference_title: >-

- category: Musculoskeletal
  name: Bone Destruction
  frequency: FREQUENT
  description: >-
    Destruction or remodelling of adjacent bone in 42.2% of 64 patients in one series, and bone
    destruction on MRI in 34% of 70 in another, the ribs most often.
    In a cohort of 29 patients without the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, selected for decreased joint
    motion, bone and joint changes, including erosion or destruction, were seen in 22 (75.9%); the
    source gives no separate count for erosion or destruction, and because of the selection the
    figure does not bear on the frequency band. A 2022 series of KHE of bone notes that extension
    into bone from a primary lesion elsewhere is relatively common.

- category: Lymphatic
  name: Chronic Lymphedema
  frequency: OCCASIONAL
  description: >-
    Confirmed by lymphoscintigraphy in 13 of 118 patients (11%) followed for at least three years,
    in the limb on the side of the tumour.
    The cohort's authors call chronic lymphoedema a common sequela of KHE that can occur
    independently of the Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon and sirolimus treatment; the frequency band
    here follows the 11%. In a lymphoscintigraphy series of 25 patients, 22 of the 24 with a limb
    tumour had abnormal findings, a group whose selection the abstract does not describe; whether it
    shares patients with the cohort of 118 is not known. On follow-up imaging, at an interval the
    abstract does not give, lymphatic drainage did not improve significantly in five of six patients
    and returned to normal in one, who had had a partial obstruction.

imaging_findings:
- name: Ill-Defined Infiltrative Mass
  modality: MRI
  imaging_finding_term:
    preferred_term: ill-defined, infiltrative soft-tissue mass
  description: >-
    On MRI, KHE usually has ill-defined margins, crosses tissue planes and shows diffuse enhancement
    with adjacent fat stranding in unusual locations. The 2020 review calls MRI the usual first-line
    study because deep infiltration may not be apparent on examination or ultrasound, while the
    authors of a 2023 series call ultrasound the first choice for assessing KHE but note that it
    cannot clearly show the infiltrating part. In a series of 12 children studied by CT or MRI, 8 of
    the 10 tumours with images were locally invasive and involved two or more adjacent organs, 7
    were infiltrative and 3 were well-defined solid masses. In a 64-patient MRI series, 28 (43.8%)
    had enhancing, infiltrative soft-tissue thickening, and ill-defined infiltrative lesions were
    more likely before 6 months of age. Against this, a 2023 comparison table gives well-defined
    margins on MRI for rapidly involuting congenital haemangioma, and a 2023 series, citing earlier
    work, describes infantile haemangioma on MRI as regular and well defined, without significant
    destruction of adjacent bone.
  notes: >-
    Left without a bound term. Of the 144 hits of runoak -i sqlite:obo:ncit search "l~margin", seven
    lie in the NCIT imaging-finding branch: three circumferential-margin-by-MRI terms and four
    nodule-margin terms, of which the one for an ill-defined margin, Poorly Marginated Nodule
    (NCIT:C157664), NCIT defines for a lung nodule. Infiltrative Tumor Margin (NCIT:C137710) and
    Infiltrating Tumor Margins Present (NCIT:C53992) are outside the branch, and "l~infiltrat" (161
    hits) and "l~ill-defined" (7 hits) return no term in it. The 12-patient series combined CT and
    MRI.
  evidence:
  - reference: PMID:32014025
    reference_title: >-
      Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma: current knowledge and future perspectives.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: HUMAN_CLINICAL
    snippet: >-
      On MRI scans, KHEs usually exhibit ill-defined margins and are characterized by multiplanar
      involvement, diffuse enhancement, and adjacent fat stranding in unusual locations,
      iso-intensity relative to adjacent muscle on T1-weighted imaging, hyperintensity on
      T2-weighted imaging
    explanation: >-
      The 2020 review: on MRI, KHE usually has ill-defined margins, multiplanar involvement, diffuse
      enhancement and fat stranding, isointense to muscle on T1 and hyperintense on T2.
  - reference: PMID:32014025
    reference_title: >-
      Kaposiform hemangioendothelioma: current knowledge and future perspectives.
    supports: SUPPORT
    directness: DIRECT
    quote_role: REVIEW_SYNTHESIS
    evidence_source: OTHER
    snippet: >-
      Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is generally first-line assessment because the deep
      infiltrating nature of KHE may not be apparent on physical exam or on ultrasound.
    explanation: >-
      MRI is the usual first study because deep infiltration may not be seen on examination or
      ultrasound.

    explanation: >-

      adjacent organs.

- name: T2 Hyperintense Signal
  modality: MRI
  imaging_finding_term:
    preferred_term: T2 hyperintense signal relative to muscle
    term:
      id: NCIT:C182328
      label: Hyperintensity
  description: >-
    On MRI, KHE is hyperintense to muscle on T2-weighted images. In a 64-patient series every lesion
    was also hypo- or isointense on T1-weighted images, and the 2020 review describes isointensity
    on T1. T2 hyperintensity was found in all 9 imaged by MRI in a 12-patient series
    (heterogeneously, with nearly isointense regions in four) and in all 4 imaged by MRI in a 2023
    series of 27 infants (unevenly); the 12-patient abstract and the 2023 series give no T1 signal.
    A 2018 series of 25, with 22 imaged by MRI, differs on T1, with 15 isointense and 7 slightly
    hyperintense, and found heterogeneous or slightly hyperintense T2 signal with speckled
    hypointense foci in 17 (77%), which its authors call a feature unique to KHE.
  notes: >-
    Bound to Hyperintensity (NCIT:C182328), which NCIT defines as high intensity on any imaging
    scan, not specifically on T2-weighted images or relative to muscle; runoak -i sqlite:obo:ncit
    search "l~hyperintens" returns it as the only hit in the NCIT imaging-finding branch; the other
    hit, MVAI - Hyperintensity T2-weighted Images (NCIT:C191061), is a questionnaire item outside
    the branch.

- name: Heterogeneous Contrast Enhancement
  modality: MRI
  imaging_finding_term:
    preferred_term: heterogeneous contrast enhancement
  description: >-
    After contrast, KHE enhances heterogeneously in most reports: heterogeneously and intensely in 8
    of the 10 tumours with CT or MRI in a 12-patient series (mildly in one), heterogeneously in 1 of
    the 2 with contrast MRI in a 2023 series, and diffusely and heterogeneously more often than
    tufted angioma among the 50 with MRI in a 2019 comparison; the 2023 authors, citing earlier
    work, note that most infantile haemangiomas enhance homogeneously with clear boundaries. In a
    2018 series of 25, enhancement was notable in 15 and moderate in 3 of the 18 with contrast MRI,
    and feeding or draining vessels, seen as flow voids on T2 or linear enhancing vessels on
    enhanced CT or MRI, were found in 15. Signal voids are reported in 2 patients of the 12-patient
    series (9 had MRI), whose authors call them infrequent, flow voids in 2 of the 4 with MRI in the
    2023 series, and as occasional in a 2023 comparison table. MRI with and without gadolinium also
    defines the extent of involvement and the response to treatment.
  notes: >-
    Left without a bound term. Of the 131 hits of runoak -i sqlite:obo:ncit search "l~enhanc",
    eleven lie in the NCIT imaging-finding branch, and none names heterogeneous
    or diffuse enhancement: Enhancing Lesion (NCIT:C113842) is defined as a well-defined area of
    increased signal after contrast, and Gadolinium-Enhancing Lesion is its child; Non-mass-like
    Enhancement (NCIT:C160918) and Clustered Ring Enhancement are breast-MRI descriptors; the
    late-gadolinium terms name delayed accumulation of contrast; Acoustic Enhancement is an
    ultrasound artifact; and Non-Enhancing Lesion is the opposite. Gadolinium Enhancement
    (NCIT:C180560) is an imaging procedure, outside the branch. The 12-patient and 2018 series
    combined CT and MRI.
